events.description: The first national democratic election open to all races marks a major change.

events.title: Pathfinder lands on Mars
events.description: The mission reaches the surface carrying the small Sojourner rover.

what_happened_next.text:
By February 1999, one dollar in Microsoft had become about $14.56 and one dollar in Intel about $7.06; Disney reached about $2.27. Microsoft and Intel far outpaced the U.S. share basket in this window, while Disney still more than doubled. These large gains hide the bumps along the way and belong only to these particular five years.

The businesses were changing, too. Windows 95 sold seven million copies in its first five weeks. Intel introduced the Pentium II, a new processor for business computers. Disney added ABC and ESPN through its 1996 acquisition. Those milestones show products and businesses reaching many customers, but no one event can explain a whole stock return.

The period also included South Africa’s first national election open to all races and the Pathfinder mission’s arrival on Mars. A share basket spread money across many companies; it did not match Microsoft or Intel here, but offered less dependence on any one business. At the start, there was no way to know which company would become the standout.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: The Fed was beginning to raise short-term rates, entertainment companies were combining, and computer makers were selling new products.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The chosen technology shares gained much more than the broad basket. The basket put less money in those winners, but it also relied on more than one business succeeding.
reflection.what_faded_away: A small initial interest-rate increase did not tell you the final ranking. An Olympic victory and a takeover contest were interesting news, but not a map of future returns.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: Nobody knew these exact gains in advance. Today’s familiarity with Microsoft and Intel can make their earlier risks easier to overlook.

hot:1994-02:microsoft.text: Microsoft launched Windows 95 on August 24, 1995, and sold seven million copies in its first five weeks. The new operating system gave Microsoft a widely used version of Windows for home and business computers, supporting demand for its other software.

hot:1994-02:intel.text: On May 7, 1997, Intel introduced Pentium II chips for business PCs and workstations. The new processor offered faster performance and features for graphics-heavy tasks, giving computer makers another choice as customers sought more powerful machines.

hot:1994-02:disney.text: Disney completed its purchase of Capital Cities/ABC on February 9, 1996. The deal added ABC broadcasting and ESPN to Disney’s parks, films and television business, creating more ways to make money from programs, advertising and sports.
